summary_html: Child achieves **permanency through legal guardianship** or kinship care. Federal programs provide funding parity with adoption for approved relatives.

case_law.method: v1.1.0 case-law rebuild: authorities selected per decision point, each opinion retrieved from CourtListener and read; holding and quote taken from the opinion text; independently re-verified before release. Previous keyword-matched Justia listings were removed.

key_cases.holding: The court affirmed termination, holding that the juvenile court adequately considered and permissibly rejected both a kinship placement and long-term guardianship with foster families before concluding that termination was strictly necessary.
key_cases.relevance: It shows in detail how a juvenile court must evaluate permanent guardianship as an alternative to termination, and when rejecting it is defensible.
key_cases.quote: Whether the juvenile court correctly concluded there was no feasible alternative to terminating Mother's . . . parental rights is a mixed question of fact and law

key_cases.holding: The Court reversed the court of appeals and reinstated the termination order, holding that the juvenile court's best-interest determination — including its rejection of permanent guardianship with the grandmother in favor of adoption — was supported by the evidence and not against its clear weight.
key_cases.relevance: The majority and dissent squarely debate when permanent guardianship is an adequate alternative to termination, making it the leading recent authority on that choice.
key_cases.quote: Because the juvenile court's best interest determination was supported by the evidence, we reverse.

key_cases.holding: The Utah Supreme Court affirmed the court of appeals' disavowal of the 'almost automatically' line of cases and held that the statutory 'strictly necessary' requirement is not a separate third element but a mandatory part of the best-interest inquiry, so a juvenile court must expressly consider feasible alternatives to termination.
key_cases.relevance: Because termination is not strictly necessary where a permanent guardianship would equally protect the child, this case is the gateway authority for guardianship as a permanency alternative.
key_cases.quote: as part of that inquiry, a court must specifically address whether termination is strictly necessary to promote the child's welfare and best interest

key_cases.holding: The court disavowed its 'almost automatically' line of cases, held that the statutory 'strictly necessary' requirement is analyzed as part of the best-interest element rather than as a separate third element, held that best interest must therefore be applied more thoroughly and independently than earlier cases suggested, and remanded for reconsideration — the decision the Utah Supreme Court affirmed in 2020.
key_cases.relevance: By requiring an independent best-interest analysis rather than an inference from grounds, it is the decision that obliges a juvenile court to weigh guardianship and other permanency options short of termination.
key_cases.quote: we conclude that courts should analyze the "strictly necessary" language as part of the "best interest" element of our historical test

key_cases.holding: The Court affirmed, holding that the juvenile court had subject matter jurisdiction because the mother voluntarily placed K.F. in state custody, that the order ending reunification and setting a goal of individualized permanency was final and appealable and appropriate where compelling reasons ruled out reunification, adoption, guardianship and kinship placement, and that the juvenile court's findings on service-plan compliance and on DCFS's reasonable efforts were owed broad discretion and were not clearly in error.
key_cases.relevance: Individualized permanency is available only where there is a compelling reason to rule out reunification, adoption, guardianship and kinship placement, so this case defines the outer boundary of the guardianship and kinship track.
key_cases.quote: appellate courts defer to juvenile courts on matters of credibility, and juvenile courts have broad discretion in determining whether reasonable reunification efforts were made

extended_foster_care_age: To age 21, only while the juvenile court orders DCFS to keep serving the young adult (Utah Code 80-1-102(56)(b)(i); 78A-6-120(1)(a)). A young adult who is 18 or older but younger than 21 and in DCFS custody on abuse, neglect, or dependency grounds may petition the juvenile court to be removed from division custody, and the court reviews that petition within 14 days; if removed, the young adult may petition within 90 days to re-enter division custody, and the juvenile court shall order the division to take custody (Utah Code 80-3-503)
